title: The Tokyo Club with McQueen: floor shows and reading the acts
summary: Watts moves to Alice McQueen's band at the Tokyo Club, where his reading ability handled floor-show music, and a small Dixieland group played in the ballroom between sets.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Yeah, see. In the 30's, you see.

Yeah, but nothing but money, plenty of money. Plenty of money, plenty of money in circulation. We made a lot of tips, 1750 was the salary, but you made a lot of tips. Oh, that was good, Sam. You made a lot of tips, see. Yeah, tips, yeah. Well alright, I got Harrison Wood there with Tommy Brooks and his brother, I didn't like the idea of Gene Brooks, that's the banjo man, that was Tommy's brother. See, Tommy on piano and the poor on banjo, and I don't know, they looked like they wanted to have their way about everything. And one of the saxophone players, he quit and went on back to Houston, he was from Houston. But now this band over here at the Tokyo, the lead of the band, the drummer named McQueen, I think Alice McQueen. Yeah, I heard him.
Yeah. You talk about him all the time.

Yeah. Well he was from Harps, he had this band over here, see. You understand? Yeah. And so, Pearson stayed, see, he stayed over here with Tommy, see. And then I went on over here with this man, because he had a Tommy, and he was from Houston, he had a trumpet player, he had a fine band from Houston. But they couldn't dig the flow show. Now that's where my little reading ability came in handy, see. Because they had a flow show that they booked from Dallas and Oklahoma City. After Tokyo, Cesar Ramona was nothing but the girls dancing with the men. But over here they had the girls dancing with the men for them tickets, and plus they give them two and three flow shows a night. See. And some ass. Well, dancing and all, man. And they had their music. If you made one wrong number, well you throw the act. You hear it from them and you had to rehearse. Well alright, their trumpet player couldn't see at all. So you know, me with my little spelling ability, you know, I went over there and in their time, see, I could, when they rehearsed the show, well, after I run over a number, not bragging, I don't care what kind of manuscript it was, when I run over it twice, I had it. You could kick your band off. See, I didn't have to have no help, you don't have to come over here and help me. Yeah, big year. Just go ahead. Good remembrance. You know what I understand? I see them notes there, and I see this, and I see that different time, alright, they might start up, man, you know, maybe in three, four times. And then maybe, after you play maybe 10 or 12 bars, they're allowed to jump to two full times, you understand? The dancing, the way that goes. See, when you end up, you're playing a march for a few bars, you understand? See? And when they throw up their foot, you have two girls, three girls and two men dancing. And when they throw up their foot, if that trumpet player is supposed to be on, be on, be on, be natural above the staff or high C, you gotta be there. Yeah. Cause if you don't, they take it down, alright, let's try that again. I said, look ahead. But they paid good money, that seat. Now that was $25, with McQueen. See, 1750 over there with Tommy. So, oh man, I worked in just fine with them. And then they wanted me to feature myself now and then. Oh man, they used to, at intermission time, we used to get a little Dixieland group, and the big boss, what run this, Tokyo, they make us come in at the ball. You understand, see? And just serenade the people sitting around at the ball that don't care about the nightclub back there. You understand, see? Yes, sir. And that old trumpet of mine, I didn't know where the mute was then, but I'd get me old Coke bottle, you know? And I'd put in that man, get that man, say with that drummer, you know? And we had a fine bass man. And Addison McQueen didn't have no banjo, he had a guitar man, see? And we'd get that man, and one of the players could double on the mandolin. And we'd get back there, that ball man, I swear, and when we'd start jamming them numbers, it'd sound better than the whole band back in the ballroom. You know, and we used to do that, you know, an old bossy, you know. Put some flips on us. Yeah, if he didn't put some flips on us, man, when we got off at night, you know, just about five of us, see, you know, come out the big band, he'd say, well, all right, here's a fifth, a tiny one. Dixieland. Yeah, here's a fifth, go ahead. And then he'd tell us, all right, now you can hear your music. Pass the hat, Watts, or John, or call anybody's name in the group, you know, pass your hat. All right, you know, heard it, it ain't free. He was big, someone gone too. And I can't think of that man's name, two brothers from this place. You know, Ixamagun.
